passages.text: PUERPERAL FEVER, a fever which seizes women soon after delivery, commonly on the second or third day, with a shivering, a great pain and swelling of the belly, and a quick pulse.
It is often fatal, and in some years it rages as an epidemic, especially in the lying-in hospitals of great cities, where it has carried off great numbers of women.
Some authors have ascribed it to a translation of the milk from the breasts to the belly; others to a peculiar constitution of the atmosphere.

Dr Alexander Gordon of Aberdeen, in a treatise published in 1795, maintained that the disease is propagated by a specific contagion, and that it is carried from one patient to another by the midwife or the physician who attends her.
This opinion has not been generally received by the profession.
Dr Gordon recommends copious and early bleeding at the beginning of the disease, followed by purging.

Postpartum infections, also known as childbed fever and puerperal fever, are bacterial infections of the female reproductive tract after childbirth or miscarriage. Signs and symptoms usually include a fever, chills, lower abdominal pain, and possibly bad-smelling vaginal discharge.
The infection is caused by bacteria, often several types together, including streptococci.
Caesarean section is the main risk factor. Other risks include long labour and early rupture of the membranes.
Before modern hygiene, childbed fever was common in maternity hospitals and killed many mothers.
In 1795 Alexander Gordon of Aberdeen concluded that the fever was carried from patient to patient by the doctors and midwives who attended them.
In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis in Vienna showed that hand washing with a chlorine solution by doctors greatly reduced deaths from the fever. His findings were widely rejected in his lifetime.
Treatment is with antibiotics, often given through a vein, such as clindamycin with gentamicin.

reasons: The Wikipedia title is Postpartum infections, but its first sentence names puerperal fever and childbed fever.
Rare terms appear in both: Alexander Gordon, Aberdeen, 1795.
Ignaz Semmelweis scores well but covers the man more than the disease.

alignments.label: Fever after childbirth

britannica.quote: a fever which seizes women soon after delivery

alignments.note: Same disease. Change in language only.

alignments.label: Deaths in hospitals

britannica.quote: especially in the lying-in hospitals of great cities

wikipedia.quote: common in maternity hospitals and killed many mothers

alignments.note: Both tie the disease to hospitals. Lying-in hospitals are maternity hospitals.

alignments.label: Milk in the belly

britannica.quote: a translation of the milk from the breasts to the belly

wikipedia.quote: The infection is caused by bacteria

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Milk does not move to the belly. Bacteria cause the fever.

alignments.label: The atmosphere

britannica.quote: a peculiar constitution of the atmosphere

wikipedia.quote: carried from patient to patient by the doctors and midwives

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. The air of a season did not cause the epidemics. The hands of the attendants did.

alignments.label: Carried by attendants

britannica.quote: carried from one patient to another by the midwife or the physician

wikipedia.quote: carried from patient to patient by the doctors and midwives

alignments.note: Gordon's 1795 claim holds. Both texts give the same name, place and year.

alignments.label: A specific contagion
alignments.note: A contagion passes between patients, but more than one kind of bacterium can cause the fever.

alignments.label: Doctors reject the idea

britannica.quote: This opinion has not been generally received

wikipedia.quote: His findings were widely rejected in his lifetime

alignments.note: Inference: Semmelweis met the same refusal as Gordon. The 1817 text records the refusal correctly.

alignments.label: Bleeding
alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Bleeding weakens the patient and does not stop the infection.

alignments.label: Hand washing

wikipedia.quote: hand washing with a chlorine solution

alignments.note: Semmelweis made his discovery thirty years after this edition.

suggestedQuestions: Who first said that doctors carried puerperal fever?
What did the 1817 entry think caused the fever?

Who first said that doctors carried puer.answer: Both texts name Alexander Gordon of Aberdeen, who said in 1795 that the midwife or physician carried the disease from one patient to another [B4] [W5]. The 1817 entry adds that the profession did not accept his view [B5]. Semmelweis later showed in 1847 that hand washing reduced deaths [W6].

What did the 1817 entry think caused the.answer: It reports two views: milk moving from the breasts to the belly, or a peculiar state of the atmosphere [B3]. It also gives Gordon's view of a specific contagion [B4]. Wikipedia says bacteria cause the infection, often several types together [W2].
